e.t: This word means “unrighteousness”: conduct or a condition marked by wrongness rather than what is right before God. It can also be rendered “wickedness,” emphasizing morally evil behavior. As a noun, it names the wrong itself, not merely an isolated mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 25 times, including passages that speak of people characterized by wrongdoing and of wicked acts. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “shame” or “shamefulness”—the condition of disgrace, dishonor, or humiliation. It identifies something viewed as shameful rather than expressing an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, showing that it can describe shame connected with a person’s conduct, reputation, or exposed condition. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word refers to an ascension or a taking up. It describes movement upward, especially the act of being taken up from one place or state to another. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 9:51, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains the idea of ascent or removal upward, rather than a general reference to ordinary travel or movement.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to fill up” or “to fill up in turn.” It describes completing or supplying what is needed so that something becomes full, with the added idea of filling another portion in response or succession. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Colossians 1:24. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its sentence and context.

me: Verb, Future, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to measure in return” or “to return.” It describes an action given back in response, with the idea that something is measured or rendered back rather than simply offered once. The word appears one time in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 6:38. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a returned measure or response. This meaning comes from its lexical definition and its single recorded occurrence.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, first, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to cease to be” or “to die.” It describes someone who is no longer living or has come to an end. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:24. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning points to passing out of one state of existence and no longer continuing in the former condition.

This word means “revelation”: the making known of something that was previously hidden or not fully seen. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 18 times, and its range includes truths and purposes made known to people. The central idea is uncovering or communicating what could not be understood or recognized without being revealed. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word describes harsh treatment—an unsparing lack of gentleness or restraint. It points to a severe way of dealing with someone or something, rather than to ordinary care or moderation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 2:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the idea of treating something harshly and without sparing it.

This word means “firm,” describing something established, dependable, and not easily moved. It can characterize a condition that remains secure rather than changing or collapsing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including uses in Romans, 2 Corinthians, Hebrews, and 2 Peter. Its repeated use across these writings presents firmness as a quality of stability and endurance. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what person, promise, hope, or arrangement the surrounding passage applies it to.

Boaz is a personal name: it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the word is rendered “Boaz” and occurs three times across two verses, appearing in Matthew 1:5 and Luke 3:32. Its function is therefore to identify the person named Boaz, not to express a general concept, command, or character trait.

This word refers to a crown or diadem, an ornamental headpiece worn on the head. It names a visible crown rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Revelation. The word’s basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines who wears the crown and what significance it has there.

e.t: This word means “to wait for,” describing patient expectation of someone or something that is still to come. It can express remaining in readiness rather than acting immediately, with attention directed toward the anticipated arrival or fulfillment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including passages concerning people waiting, a future outcome, and the fulfillment of God’s promise. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains expectant waiting for what has not yet arrived.

e.t: This word means “be possible” or “it is possible.” It expresses that something can happen or may be the case, rather than declaring that it certainly will happen. In a sentence, it functions as a statement about possibility or what may be permitted by circumstances. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 13:33. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains the affirmation that something is possible.

me: Verb, Aorist, Passive, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “be glorified”: to receive honor, recognition, or praise. It describes someone being shown to be glorious rather than someone actively giving glory. In the Greek New Testament, it appears two times, both in 2 Thessalonians 1. Its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains the receiving or being displayed in glory. The word therefore points to the result of glorification, not merely to an inward quality or private status.

e.t: This word describes the action of jumping or leaping upward. It presents a sudden, energetic movement rather than simply standing or walking. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its meaning is focused and specific: a person springs upward with noticeable force and movement. The word itself describes the physical action, while the surrounding verse determines the full significance of that action.

e.t: This word means “to provoke,” “to irritate,” or “to stir up.” It describes stirring another person emotionally or prompting a reaction, whether through irritation or strong encouragement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its meaning is focused rather than broadly varied across many passages. The word appears in 2 Corinthians 9:2 and Colossians 3:21, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word refers to a blessing or praise. It can describe a spoken blessing, an expression of praise, or the blessing received from God. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 16 times, including passages about God’s blessing through Christ and words that sound favorable or flattering. Its exact force depends on the sentence, but the central idea is a blessing expressed in words or bestowed as a benefit.

This word means “living creature” or “living thing.” It refers broadly to something that has life, rather than to one particular kind of animal or being. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 23 times, with most occurrences in Revelation, where it identifies the living beings around God’s throne. It can also describe creatures generally, showing that its basic sense is flexible and depends on the surrounding sentence. The word itself emphasizes life and living existence, while the context determines what kind of creature or living thing is meant.

John is a personal name, referring to people named John in the Greek New Testament. It is not a general description or title, but identifies a particular person whenever it appears. The name occurs 135 times in this corpus, beginning in Matthew and continuing through Revelation. Several different passages use it for John the Baptist, while other passages refer to John among Jesus’ disciples or to other people bearing the same name. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which John is meant in a particular passage.

e.t: This word means “to reconcile”: to bring parties from hostility or separation into a restored relationship. It can describe the action of reconciling as well as people who “have been reconciled” or “were reconciled.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, especially in Romans and 2 Corinthians, where reconciliation is presented as something accomplished between people and God or between separated people. Its exact emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to get or possess something. It describes acquiring or having something as one’s own, whether through obtaining it or holding it. The word appears seven times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is established across several passages rather than being limited to one setting. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on gaining something, owning it, or securing it.

This word means “brightness,” referring to a shining quality or visible radiance. It is a noun describing the brilliance that comes from something bright or luminous. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:13. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains the same: an intense, noticeable light or splendor. The word therefore points to brightness as something seen, rather than to a command, action, or inward attitude.

This Greek New Testament word means “washing,” referring to the act or process of cleansing. It identifies washing itself rather than adding a separate idea such as the person who performs it. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Ephesians and once in Titus, showing the same basic meaning in both recorded uses. Its fuller significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This word means “from a distance” or “from afar.” It describes something seen, done, or located at a considerable remove rather than nearby. As an adverb, it tells the reader how far away an action or observation occurs. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 14 times across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Revelation. Its basic sense remains consistent, while the surrounding verse determines what person, place, or thing is being viewed or approached from afar.

This word means “mixture”: a combination formed by bringing different substances or elements together. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 19:39. The word itself identifies something combined rather than remaining pure or separate, but its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Here, “mixture” is the complete lexical sense available for understanding this uncommon New Testament word.

“Nicolaitans” refers to a named group mentioned in the New Testament. It is a group designation rather than a general word describing a quality, action, or object. The term appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Revelation 2:6 and Revelation 2:15. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the people but does not establish their beliefs, conduct, or significance. Those details must be understood from the passages in which the group is mentioned.

This word means “likeness,” referring to a resemblance or similarity between things. It describes the quality of being like something else rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 3:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its basic sense remains a likeness: a correspondence or resemblance that connects one thing with another.

This word refers to orphans—children who have lost their parents or are without parental care. It is a noun describing people in that vulnerable condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, including passages in John and James. Its basic meaning points to those who lack the protection and support normally provided by parents; the surrounding verse determines how that meaning is applied in each passage.

This word means “debt”: something a person owes to another. It is a noun describing an obligation that remains unpaid or due. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, including passages that refer to financial responsibility and obligations within human relationships. The basic idea is what is owed, whether the obligation involves money or another form of rightful duty. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central meaning remains an owed obligation.

This word means “Preparation Day,” referring to a designated day connected with getting ready. It functions as a name for that day rather than as a general action of preparing. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, all in Gospel passages, showing that it is a specific calendar designation used in accounts surrounding Jesus’ death and burial. The exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central meaning remains the day identified for preparation.

This word describes being “in control of” something or being “secure.” It points to a condition of control, stability, or safety rather than uncertainty or danger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:16, and is rendered “secure.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is being firmly safe or under control.

This word means a “group”—a distinct set of people gathered or arranged together. It functions as a noun, naming a group rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both instances appearing in Mark 6:40. The word’s basic sense identifies people collectively, while the surrounding verse determines how that group is organized or what it is doing. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: a group considered as a unit.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means to prepare something beforehand or make it ready in advance. It describes an action completed ahead of the time when it will be needed, emphasizing prior arrangement rather than preparation happening at the last moment. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans and Ephesians. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central meaning remains the deliberate preparation of something beforehand.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to add (to),” describing the act of placing something additional with or upon what is already present. It can refer to increasing an amount, supplying something further, or bringing an added result. The word appears 18 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Matthew, Luke, Acts, Galatians, and Hebrews. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being added and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “first.” It identifies someone or something that comes before others in sequence, order, or position. It can also mark priority when one person or thing is placed ahead of others. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 155 times, so its exact force depends on what is being ordered or compared in each sentence. Its range extends from Matthew through Revelation, showing regular use for expressing precedence or priority.

e.t: This word means “stained,” “to corrupt,” or “to stain.” It describes something marked, polluted, or spoiled, either as a condition or as the result of an action. The word can therefore express being stained as well as causing something to become stained or corrupt. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in James and once in Jude. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word describes something commendatory or recommended—something presented favorably or offered as worthy of approval. It functions as a descriptive term rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 3:1. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being commended or recommended there, but the word’s central idea is favorable presentation or approval.

This word refers to an “eye” or a “hole.” It names a small opening or the eye itself, depending on how it is used in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:25. The word’s basic sense is therefore concise: it identifies an eye or a hole rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. The surrounding verse determines which of these related senses is intended there.

e.t: This word means “to blind” or “to cause blindness.” It describes making someone unable to see, whether referring to physical sight or, in Scripture’s broader use, the loss of spiritual perception. As a verb, it expresses the action of blinding rather than naming a person or condition. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in John, 2 Corinthians, and 1 John. The precise force in each passage depends on its surrounding context, but the central idea remains the removal or blocking of sight.

This word means “rain”: water that falls from the sky. It refers to rainfall itself and is used as an ordinary term for that weather event, rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in Acts, Hebrews, James, and Revelation. Its occurrences are found at Acts 14:17, Acts 28:2, Hebrews 6:7, James 5:18, and Revelation 11:6. The surrounding verse determines what is said about the rain.

This word means “under,” referring to a position or place beneath something else. It describes something located lower than, covered by, or beneath another object or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, showing a repeated spatial use rather than a broad abstract meaning. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is said to be above or beneath it.

This word means “winter,” referring to the cold season of the year. It is a noun used for the season itself, including the conditions associated with it, such as cold weather and difficult travel. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across six verses. The word appears in the Gospels, Acts, and 2 Timothy, showing its ordinary use for a recognized season rather than a symbolic meaning established by the word itself.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “be angry”: it describes anger or an angry response. It is used to express that someone is angry, rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 7:23; the surrounding verse context is needed to explain the particular force of that occurrence. Its basic sense remains the expression of anger.

Chrysolite is the name of a precious stone. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Revelation 21:20. Its meaning is a specific stone name rather than an action, quality, or relationship. The English rendering is also “chrysolite,” preserving the mineral name instead of replacing it with a broader description. Since this word appears only once, its normal lexical sense is simply the named stone.

This word refers to a household or to a servant in a household. It describes someone connected with the domestic household setting, with particular emphasis on household service rather than a general kind of service. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 24:45. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on household service and responsibility.
